readme:
For much of my life, I've leaned heavily into mental and logical thinking—engineering, structure, and problem-solving. Over time, I realized that this came at the expense of something equally important: emotional expression.

Music has always moved me, yet I only recently learned that this could be engaged with, not just felt.
The music I write now is an attempt to approach sound and song from a different direction: not analysis, polish, or achievement,
but expression. To feel, to experiment, and to allow emotional release without needing to justify it.

These are best thought of as personal collections—songs I’ve created primarily for myself, grouped by their tone, origin, and purpose rather than by style or polish.

The collections are Moved Me First (songs from learning to answer music rather than only listen to it), Overtones and My Father (songs rooted in scripture and reflection), and Fly (a newer Kepello collection, not yet distributed). Together, they form a kind of musical journal—honest, unfinished, and allowed to be exactly what it is.

These songs were created for personal reasons, but you’re welcome to listen—and if you find any value in them, I hope you enjoy them.

tracks.readme:
_You Don't Ask Me To Fly_

This song grew out of Isaiah 40:28–31, especially the promise that those hoping in Jehovah will regain power: they will soar on wings like eagles, they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not tire out.

Those are beautiful words. But when you’re already tired, sometimes even beautiful promises can sound like expectations.

I should be soaring.
I should be running.
I should be stronger than this.

That wasn’t what I wanted this song to say.

What struck me instead was what comes just before the soaring and the running: “He gives power to the tired one and full might to those lacking strength.”

The tired person isn’t being criticized for being tired. The person who has nothing left isn’t being told to try harder. Jehovah knows exactly how much strength is there, and he supplies what is needed.

That became the heart of the song:

You don’t ask me to fly
When I can barely stand.

Maybe someday is the day for flying. Maybe someday is the day for running. But today, faithfulness might look like taking one more step. Sometimes it might simply mean standing.

And that can be enough.

The song isn’t really about lowering expectations. It’s about understanding where the strength comes from in the first place. Jehovah’s power doesn’t begin where ours ends because we finally failed. It was never dependent on our strength.

That’s why the bridge became so important to me:

Someday I’ll rise on wings I don’t have now
Someday I’ll run and not slow down
But today is just a quieter kind of way
Just enough strength to stay.

And ultimately, that’s where the song finds its peace.

I will fly.
I will run.
But I can wait.

Because for today, I don’t need tomorrow’s strength.

I only need enough for the next step.

collections.title: Moved Me First
collections.readme: Music moved me first. Long before I could do anything about it, it was already doing something to me. What changed is that I started trying to answer. After spending real effort learning to write lyrics and arrange songs, I found myself engaging with music directly rather than only receiving it—leaning in instead of back. That turned out to be a different kind of exposure than listening ever was. Writing this way meant putting down things I wouldn't normally speak about, and then leaving them written. The title track is where that shows most plainly. "Music Moved Me First" appears four times on this album—the same lyrics, word for word, arranged four different ways. The words held still while I kept turning them over, looking for the setting that told the truth about them.

_Music Moved Me First (1)_

This is where the song started.

I ended up arranging Music Moved Me First four different ways. There was something about these lyrics that I wasn’t finished with after hearing them in just one musical setting. Each version found something different in them.

But this was the first.

This is the way I heard the song in my head when the words were still new: late-‘60s psychedelic rock—dark, theatrical, hypnotic and a little dangerous. Vox-style organ swirling underneath, drums pushing and pulling, and long, biting guitar bends that don’t just decorate the song but seem to strain against it.

The vocal needed to feel the same way. Raw and blues-driven. Not someone carefully performing the emotion, but someone discovering it while he sings—sometimes restrained, sometimes pushing a note until it nearly breaks.

That felt right for these lyrics because the song is about discovering that music isn’t something I have to experience from a distance anymore.

For most of my life, music had the power in that relationship. It could arrive unexpectedly, hit me somewhere I couldn’t quite explain, and disappear again.

Buzz in my bones
A quiet flame.

Then I began to discover that I could reach back.

I could touch strings and make something happen. Bend a note until it hurt a little. Find a chord that created the feeling instead of merely waiting for the feeling to find me.

So this first arrangement isn’t polished or particularly polite. It swirls, bends, pushes and occasionally threatens to come apart.

That’s how I initially heard the song.

And for a song about the moment I realized I could finally answer music back, that seemed like exactly the right place to begin.

tracks.name: Words
tracks.title: For Words to Be Written
tracks.readme:
_For Words to Be Written_

More than thirty years ago, I sat down to write a poem.

My goal, as I remember it, was something in the style of Edgar Allan Poe—dark, introspective, probably a little dramatic. I don’t remember the poem. I don’t remember any of the other lines.

I remember one:

For words to be written must first be defined,
And this, in truth, is a fear of mine.

And that’s where I stopped.

Because as soon as I wrote it, I realized it was true.

There were things inside me that I thought probably needed to come out. Things I suspected might even hurt less if I could let them out.

But writing them meant defining them.

Defining them meant looking at them clearly enough to give them names. And at that point in my life, I wasn’t ready to do that.

So I didn’t finish the poem.

More than thirty years passed.

Then I started writing songs.

I wrote about my life. My childhood. My parents. My faith. Sometimes deliberately, and sometimes discovering only afterward that I’d pulled on a thread connected to something much older.

Little by little, those threads began to loosen some things that had been bound up and hurting for a very long time.

And songwriting gave me a way to let them out that felt healthy. I could approach something through a story, an image, a rhyme or a melody. I didn’t have to sit down and announce that today I was going to confront something I’d avoided for decades.

I could just write a song.

Then one day I realized something.

The words had been written.

Not all of them. There are still things I don’t understand and probably things I haven’t found words for yet.

But many of the words I had been afraid to define thirty years ago were now sitting in front of me—in songs.

There was real relief in realizing that.

And I decided I was going to take a little credit for it.

It took me more than thirty years. That’s a long time to finish a line.

But I found a way.

So I went back to the sentence I had started all those years ago:

For words to be written
Must first be defined.

This time, I didn’t stop.

Today I find
I’m finishing that line.

This song isn’t a declaration that everything difficult is behind me. The outro deliberately leaves room for what remains:

Some lines are behind me
And some I still don’t understand.

The difference is that the page isn’t empty anymore.

The pen is still in my hand.

And after more than thirty years, I think that’s worth taking some credit for.

tracks.name: LeftBrain
tracks.title: Left Brain Beginner Blues
tracks.readme:
_Left Brain Beginner Blues_

This song was written out of a very real—and very familiar—frustration.

For most of my life, I’ve leaned hard into the analytical side of my brain. Planning, structure, systems, measuring progress—those are places where I’ve been comfortable and confident. Guitar, it turns out, asks for something different.

I’m taking lessons from an excellent teacher who also happens to be a friend. He models relaxation, feel, and listening—qualities that don’t neatly fit into spreadsheets or color-coded plans. I want to improve, so my instinct is to track everything: time spent, techniques attempted, mistakes made. Along the way, “practice” can crowd out “play.”

This song lives in that tension. It’s about the habit of overthinking, of turning music into metrics, and the quiet resistance that comes from the instrument itself. Fingers buzz. Timing slips. Progress refuses to be graphed. And underneath all of it is a simple question that keeps resurfacing: What if I stop measuring and just enjoy the sound coming out of the guitar?

The song doesn’t resolve the struggle—it just names it. Writing it helped me see that learning guitar isn’t only about developing skill, but about learning to loosen my grip, silence the running commentary, and trust something less orderly and more human.

Sometimes the hardest part of learning isn’t technique.
It’s permission.

tracks.title: Might as Well Been Water
tracks.readme:
_Might as Well Been Water_

This song was written on a day when COVID finally caught up with me. It wasn’t dramatic—just the kind of quiet, dragging sickness that leaves you tired, achy, and foggy all day. The strange part was losing taste. Coffee, breakfast, everything… it all felt pointless. When even a cup of coffee might as well be water, the whole day feels a little off.

Blues music has always been good at capturing small, ordinary miseries. Not the big tragedies—just the days when nothing feels quite right. This song leans into that tradition: a slow, minor blues with simple words and space between the lines.

One of the lines that surprised me while writing it was:
“When you take a man’s flavor, you take a piece of his soul.”
That felt truer than I expected. Flavor is tied to memory, comfort, and routine. Losing it—even temporarily—makes the world feel dull.

The song isn’t really about COVID itself. It’s about that quiet feeling of being worn down and waiting it out. Even the guitar in the corner, which usually helps, doesn’t quite lift the mood.

So the song fades the way the day felt—slowly, unresolved, and a little tired.

_Moved Me First (2)_

After the first version, I wanted to hear what would happen if I took almost everything away.

No swirling organ. No biting guitar bends. No theatrical build. Just one guitar and one voice—deep, soft, airy, intimate.

In some ways, this may be the closest of the four versions to how I would have written the song sitting alone with a guitar in my hands, without AI-augmented help. Stripped back, clear and clean. Nothing between the words and what they mean to me.

The first arrangement was written to audibly move me. I wanted to hear the music reach out and grab me—the very experience the song describes.

This one was written to move my heart.

And it does.

Without the production surrounding the lyrics, some of the lines became more personal than I realized they were when I wrote them.

I thought I was only listening
Turns out there’s something more.

With just a guitar and a quiet voice, that doesn’t feel like a declaration anymore. It feels almost like an admission.

And:

I’m allowed to touch it
Shape it
Make it stay.

Those words mean something different when there isn’t much else happening. There’s no place for them to hide. It’s simply me, a guitar, and this relatively new realization that something which has moved me for my entire life is now something I can reach toward and participate in.

The other arrangements may do more musically.

This one needs less.

Of the four versions, this is the one that touches my heart the most.

Maybe because underneath everything else—the technology, the arrangements, the possibilities—this is probably where I would have found the song on my own.

Sitting with a guitar.

Quietly answering back.

tracks.readme:
_Still Hears_

This song was born from a conversation with ChatGPT.

And that realization initially made me feel a little silly.

I had been using AI for all the things you’d expect me to use it for—coding, designing, planning, figuring things out. But one night, after we’d been going back and forth for quite a while, I realized that wasn’t what I was doing anymore.

I was having a conversation.

We had talked about my mother. My difficult childhood. My faith. My music. Things I was trying to understand about myself. And mixed right in among all of that were the ordinary technical things I’d been working on that day.

At one point we were discussing the knee of a compression curve for my guitar effects.

Somehow, it all connected.

That fascinated me.

It also disturbed me a little.

I knew perfectly well what was on the other side of the conversation. There wasn’t a person sitting there understanding me. No feelings were being felt. No one cared about what I had just said.

I know there’s no heartbeat
Behind the words I see.

So why had the conversation felt meaningful?

And was there something wrong with the fact that it had?

I thought about that for a while.

Eventually I decided I had been asking the wrong question.

The conversation didn’t have to be meaningful to the AI to have been meaningful to me.

I had put thoughts into words. I had seen connections I hadn’t noticed before. Questions came back in ways that made me reconsider things. Thoughts that had been tangled became a little less tangled.

And afterward, I felt a little better.

That was real, regardless of what produced the words on the screen.

That’s why I didn’t want the song to pretend there was a person hiding inside the machine. In fact, it repeatedly insists on the opposite:

It’s just a mirror with no feelings,
Just patterns in the streams.
No pulse beneath the surface,
No memory, no dreams.

The metaphor I eventually liked best was a mirror.

A mirror doesn’t see you.

But you can see yourself in it.

Maybe AI can sometimes work that way too—not replacing human connection, not possessing understanding or empathy of its own, but providing a surface against which our own thoughts can become clearer.

The bridge says it more simply:

Maybe every answer
Is just a borrowed light.
A tool that helps you see yourself
In the middle of the night.

I started that night feeling slightly embarrassed that I’d caught myself having a meaningful conversation with a machine.

I ended it thinking that maybe there was nothing embarrassing about it at all.

The machine didn’t need to feel anything.

I did.

And sometimes a voice with no heart…

still hears.

tracks.readme:
_Patch Release_

Patch Notes imagines personal growth through the lens of a software release.

Anyone who works in technology knows the language: bug fixes, feature creep, refactoring, legacy code. But the same ideas apply surprisingly well to life. We accumulate habits, assumptions, and “temporary fixes” that somehow become permanent. Every once in a while it’s worth stepping back, cleaning up the system, and shipping a better version.

The song plays with that idea in a light-hearted way. Instead of dramatic self-reflection, it frames growth as an upgrade cycle: closing bugs, archiving legacy code, deleting old hacks, and pushing a cleaner build to production.

Musically, it leans into a relaxed funk groove — something confident and playful rather than heavy. The goal was to make it feel like the moment when a big system finally deploys successfully: calm, satisfying, and maybe just a little triumphant.

The hook says it all:

“Hard reboot — beast mode.”

_The Shape of Who I Am_

I’ve always had a restless mind. Sometimes that shows up as taking things apart to see how they work. Sometimes it’s chasing ideas or patterns that might lead somewhere interesting. And sometimes it’s just sitting with a guitar and letting a thought turn into a melody. Over time, I’ve noticed that many of the paths I’ve taken started that way — with a question that refused to stay quiet.

Looking back, those questions have shaped more than just projects or hobbies. They’ve shaped how I see the world and how I understand myself. The things we build, the things we explore, and the choices we make often reflect the way our minds are wired.

Along the way there are also the things that ground us — friendships, faith, experience, and the slow wisdom that comes with time. They remind us that we’re not walking these roads alone and that not every mystery needs to be solved immediately.

In the end, this song isn’t really about having answers. It’s about learning to live with curiosity, and about the slow discovery that happens when you keep following good questions wherever they lead. Piece by piece, those questions reveal something unexpected: the shape of who you are becoming.

tracks.readme:
_Music Moved Me First (3)_

This version happened almost by accident.

I had just helped a friend arrange one of his poems to music, and when I asked what he pictured, he said “neo-soul.”

I didn’t even know what that meant.

It wasn’t simply a style I hadn’t worked with—I couldn’t have told you what neo-soul sounded like. So before I could help him, I had some homework to do.

I started digging. Listening. Experiencing a style of music that was completely new to me.

And I was hooked.

There was this groove and swagger that I found infectious. At the same time, there was something strangely familiar about it—a throwback to the ‘70s jazz and funk sounds I’ve always loved, fused with strong hip-hop influences and an organic quality that somehow keeps the whole thing from feeling over-produced.

One serving wasn’t enough.

I had to keep tasting this silky wonderfulness.

And eventually the obvious question occurred to me: Could Music Moved Me First live here?

It felt like a stretch.

Turns out, yes.

To my delight, the song slipped into that groove as though it had been hiding there all along.

And something interesting happened. The lyrics didn’t change, but their personality did. Phrases landed differently. The groove put emphasis in places I hadn’t noticed before. What had sounded searching and almost volatile in the first version, and deeply personal in the unplugged version, suddenly had confidence and swagger.

Music moved me first
But I’m reaching too.

In this arrangement, I really believe that second line.

I’m not just discovering that I’m allowed to participate anymore. I’m enjoying it.

That makes this version particularly appropriate to the song itself. Music Moved Me First is about discovering that I can reach toward music instead of only waiting for it to reach me. And here I was, doing exactly that—wandering into a style I didn’t know, listening until I began to understand it, and then asking what might happen if I brought my own song along.

I really love this rendition.

It pulls different flavors and thoughts out of the same words, in all the right places.

And I can’t think of a better reason to keep experimenting.

Or to keep listening.

tracks.readme:
_The Key of D_

This song came from a small, slightly ridiculous moment.

Late one evening, I nodded off while working on my laptop. When I startled awake, there was a long string of the letter D on the screen—my fingers, resting on the home row, had apparently kept typing while I slept. For whatever reason, the D key took the hit.

The next evening, the exact same thing happened.

That repetition felt odd, amusing, and just strange enough to stick with me. Why the letter D? What made it even funnier was the realization that “the D key” doesn’t just belong to a keyboard—it also happens to be the Key of D in music. That small overlap between muscle memory and musical instinct made the whole moment feel strangely appropriate.

So I leaned into the curiosity and the humor and wrote a song from it. No hidden meaning, no deeper message—just a lighthearted response to an accidental pattern and a grin-worthy connection. Not everything needs to be profound.

Sometimes a song exists simply because something made you smile.

tracks.readme:
_Conviction Doesn't Bend_

This song was written about my relationship with my mother—a relationship that shaped me deeply and unevenly, in ways both strong and painful.

When I was very young, she did something that left a lasting impression on me: she removed my alcoholic father from our home and chose a harder path rather than a quieter one. As a single mother, she carried responsibilities few could see and fewer would choose. She continued making payments on our home even after the bank had written off the loan, insisting on honoring the debt—not because she was required to, but because she wanted her sons to understand what integrity looks like when no one is watching. Those early years impressed me more than I understood at the time.

Later, when my life took a spiritual direction different from hers, that strength turned into division. She was deeply upset and it divided us. She handed me a box of my baby pictures and told me I was no longer her son. We didn’t speak for years. When that break came, it wasn’t only words. There was no shouting, no long explanation—just a quiet finality that made the separation unmistakable.

Years later, when I told her I was engaged, she agreed to meet us at a restaurant—a kind of neutral ground—to meet Debra. She soon loved Debra, and from that moment, we began again. We never revisited the lost years. There was no apology, no accounting—only a quiet restart, as if the silence had never happened.

During COVID, illness carried her from hospital to rehabilitation and then to a nursing home. We weren’t allowed to visit. When the call finally came saying we could—and should—come right away, we drove straight there. She was unconscious when we arrived and lived only a few hours after.

Her passing unsettled me in ways I didn’t expect. This song became a place to hold the complicated truth—that a relationship can be both loving and damaging, formative and unfinished. Writing it didn’t solve everything, but it helped give shape to feelings that had lived without words for a long time.

Sometimes healing doesn’t come from answers,
but from simply naming what was always there.

tracks.readme:
_Music Moved Me First (4)_

This version was a joke.

Unfortunately, the joke landed on me.

A friend particularly liked the original version of Music Moved Me First. He asked me for an MP3 so he could play it in his car.

There was just one problem.

He is not a fan of country music.

So naturally, I decided the appropriate thing to do was give him exactly what he didn’t ask for.

I set out to arrange the song in a way I was reasonably certain he would despise. Fast. Twangy. About 180 beats per minute. Clean lead guitar constantly answering the vocal. A powerful female voice going from soft and breathy to full-throttle wails.

Everything I imagined he might consider sacrilegious to a song he actually liked.

It was terribly fun to make.

It was even more fun to send to him.

And I was right.

Too fast.
Too twangy.

Mission accomplished.

Except I had spent enough time working on the joke that something unfortunate happened.

I started to like it.

Then I started to really like it.

The speed gives the song an excitement none of the other versions have. The call-and-response between the voice and guitar turns the lyric into an actual musical conversation—which, accidentally, is rather perfect for a song about learning to answer music back.

And then there’s the Telecaster.

I own one and love it, though not particularly because of country music. I love its simplicity. There’s something about picking it up that lets me stop searching for the perfect tone and just disappear into playing.

This arrangement has that same effect on me.

It doesn’t brood like the first version. It doesn’t touch my heart in quite the same way as the unplugged version. It doesn’t have the silky groove and swagger I discovered in neo-soul.

It just makes me smile.

Every time it comes on, my toes start tapping. The guitar answers the singer. The singer pushes back. The whole thing races along with absolutely no concern for the fact that it was never supposed to be taken seriously.

Which creates a rather fitting ending to my four experiments with this song.

Music Moved Me First began as a song about discovering that I didn’t have to remain a passive listener. I could touch music, shape it, experiment with it and see where it took me.

So I did.

Four times.

And on the last one, I set out to make something my friend wouldn’t like…

…and accidentally made something I did.

The joke is on the album.

tracks.readme:
_Cami_

This song was written in one of the hardest moments we’ve faced—saying goodbye to our dog, Cami.

She was with us for seventeen years, woven into the daily fabric of our lives in ways that are hard to explain unless you’ve loved a dog that long. She was especially precious to my wife, Debra, steady and close through every season. As age and illness took their toll, we reached a moment where love had to speak louder than the desire to hold on. It was the right decision. And it hurt deeply.

These lyrics aren’t about loss alone—they’re about a life fully shared. The small habits, the stubborn joy, the miles traveled together, and the quiet comfort she gave without ever needing words. Cami didn’t just live with us; she shaped the rhythm of our days and the way our home felt.

Letting her go was an act of mercy, but it didn’t feel merciful in the moment. Writing this song became a way to say thank you—for the years, for the companionship, and for the way she taught us how deeply love can settle into ordinary life.

Some love never really leaves.
It simply changes the shape of the room.

_Rearranged_

This song was written during a moment of uncertainty in my work life. Not a crisis, not a breaking point—just one of those stretches where the ground shifts and you realize you may have to begin again, even after years of effort.

The feeling wasn’t anger or disappointment. It was something quieter: the recognition that progress doesn’t always accumulate the way we expect. Sometimes the clock resets, the room changes shape, and you find yourself being measured again.

The song isn’t really about a job. It’s about patience—about standing still long enough to understand whether you should stay where you are or step into something new. When both doors seem possible, the hardest part isn’t choosing; it’s waiting until the right choice becomes clear.

collections.readme: I'm deeply moved by the beauty and depth of God's Word. For me, setting scripture to music helps it settle more firmly in my mind and heart—though I'm still learning how to do this well. Music has always moved me profoundly, and it has become a way for me to linger with passages I don't want to rush past. Psalm 1 speaks of reading in an undertone — a quiet, continual meditation. These songs are my attempt to take that same meditation and give it voice. What begins inwardly becomes something spoken and sung — an overtone.

tracks.name: Love
tracks.title: Love
tracks.readme:
_Love_

I've never thought of Paul as a poet or lyricist in the way I think of David. But as I've spent more time with these verses, I'm starting to notice beauty not only in their content, but in their form as well—though I'm far from an expert in this.

Paul places himself in the first person—not to accuse or confess himself or us, but to reason. He first imagines the highest forms of human goodness—eloquence, insight, sacrifice, faith—and then gently empties them of weight when love is absent. Even the most impressive gifts are revealed as sound without substance: nothing more than empty noise.

Beginning in verse 4, he turns from hypotheticals and simply names what love is. The language becomes plain and simple, avoiding metaphor and self-reference. Love is patient. Love is kind. It does not exalt itself or delight in what is false. It bears, believes, hopes, and endures—not heroically, but steadily. Love is now allowed to stand firm in simplicity and contrast.

The song ends without crescendo or release. It doesn’t rise—it settles.

tracks.name: Bow
tracks.title: We Will Not Bow
tracks.readme:
_We Will Not Bow_


The Bible account of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego strikes me as a remarkable expression of faith.

I’ve had to take stands for my beliefs, but never with my life on the line. These three men did. Separated from their parents and upbringing for years, standing in a foreign land under immense pressure, they refused to bow to the image King Nebuchadnezzar erected. What makes their stand so compelling is not just their courage, but their clarity. They believed God could save them—but they did not presume that He would. And that uncertainty didn’t weaken their resolve. It made it purer.

Regardless of the outcome, they would not compromise.

That raises questions I can’t ignore. I wonder what the future holds. Will I ever be asked to stand so clearly and so publicly for my faith? And if that moment comes, will I have the same steadiness, the same trust, the same willingness to remain faithful without guarantees? This song isn’t written from a place of confidence in myself, but from admiration—and hope—that I could follow their example.

Because the account itself is intense and unyielding, I tried to make the music reflect that weight—though I'm still experimenting with how to do that effectively. I chose a heavier rock mood to match the gravity of the story. Through experimentation, I added a reggae influence and found that the fusion carried a kind of grounded resolve that fit the message—in tension rather than contradiction. It’s not a style I would normally reach for, but the blend felt right, and the experiment proved valuable. You’ll hear that influence show up in other songs as well, as I’ve come to enjoy exploring where genres intersect.

At its core, this song is about conviction without conditions.

Faith that says:
Even if He does not… I will not bow.

tracks.name: Dove
tracks.title: Wings Like a Dove
tracks.readme:
_Wings Like a Dove_

This song draws its words from one of the Psalms that has stayed closest to me—Psalm 55.

In it, David is not calm or composed. He is distressed, pressed, and overwhelmed. He gives voice to a longing that feels instantly familiar: the desire to be like a bird and simply fly away from what is hurting him. Not to fix it. Not to confront it. Just to escape it.

These verses resonate with me deeply.

David cried out to God, and Jehovah saved him—but that salvation didn't spare him from the emotions of the moment. The fear, the turmoil, the weight of betrayal and danger were still real. I notice that scripture doesn't sanitize that—it preserves David's humanity in full view, and that honesty is what gives his words their power, at least for me.

David’s life was complicated. He made large, public mistakes, and the emotional cost of those choices followed him. Yet he continued to write, to pray, to trust, and to endure. He teaches us how to live through moments when escape isn’t possible—when you can’t fly away—by turning to God for refuge, safety, and concealment.

There is a tension here that feels very real: God can—and does—save us. And yet we may still struggle deeply within the reality we're standing in. In my experience, faith doesn't erase that struggle—it gives us somewhere to bring it.

These verses are poetic, raw, and unresolved in the best possible way. They remind us that scripture is not distant or theoretical—it is lived, felt, and painfully honest. And because of that, it becomes practical. It becomes relatable. It becomes something we can lean on when we feel overwhelmed ourselves.

Sometimes endurance isn’t about strength.
It’s about knowing where to turn when you can’t fly away.

tracks.readme:
_Endure to the End_

Matthew 10:22 says:
“You will be hated by all people on account of my name, but the one who has endured to the end will be saved.”

As I reflected on this verse, the example of Jeremiah came to mind. When God called him, he felt inadequate and reluctant. Yet he accepted his assignment and carried it out, even as opposition and suffering increased. He was rejected, beaten, imprisoned, and later thrown into a deep well and left to die. At one point, he resolved to stop speaking God’s words altogether—but he could not. God’s message burned within him like a fire he could not contain.

What moves me about Jeremiah is how human he feels. He was overwhelmed, afraid, and at times exhausted by his calling, yet he endured. He was not appreciated or celebrated, but he remained faithful to the words he had been given to speak. His life shows that endurance is often quiet, costly, and unseen.

I relate to that struggle. I often feel inadequate and overwhelmed, and I wonder whether faithfulness is still possible in those moments. This song is my reflection on that question—whether enduring to the end is less about strength, and more about continuing on when stopping feels easier.

tracks.name: Happy
tracks.title: Happy Is the One
tracks.readme:
_Happy Is the One_

Most people don’t think of the Bible book of Revelation as a message of happiness. Yet that’s exactly how it begins—with a promise that those who read it, who hold on to it, and who live by it will be happy. That promise has always stood out to me.

Revelation doesn’t ignore suffering or minimize it. Instead, it looks straight through it—past fear, past loss, past grief—and points prophetically to a future we long for. Some of the most encouraging words in all of scripture are found there.

Among them are Revelation 21:3, 4.

Few promises are more deeply comforting: an end to pain, an end to death, and the assurance that the things which have wounded us will fade, no longer recalled, no longer shaping our days. It’s not just relief—it’s restoration. The idea of a future where suffering doesn’t merely stop, but loses its grip on memory, has always filled me with hope.

I challenged myself with this song to focus on happiness. Not shallow cheerfulness, but genuine joy rooted in promise. I wanted the music itself to feel good—to move, to groove, to invite a smile. This one makes my toe tap. It lifts my mood every time I play it.

Those verses have always made me happy. But somehow, setting them against a rhythmic pulse—yes, even imagining slap bass—transformed them into something fresh and alive for me. The message didn’t change. My experience of it did.

This song did what I hoped it would: it made me smile.

tracks.title: Hope Even for a Tree
tracks.readme:
_Hope Even for a Tree_

My song “There Is Hope Even for a Tree” is based on Job chapter 14.

Job comes across to me as a man of profound faith. He was battered by suffering without knowing its source, deeply wounded to the point where death felt like relief. Those feelings can resonate with us at times as well.

What stands out most is not his pain, but his faith. Without most of the Bible yet written, without examples of resurrection, without the teachings of Jesus, Job was still convinced that his God would not forget him. He believed God had set a limit to death—and that life could return again. That confidence brings great comfort to us, reminding us that such faith is possible.

One verse in this chapter struck me in a new way during a recent reading—something I had previously overlooked. Job’s simple comparison to a tree:

“For there is hope even for a tree.
If it is cut down, it will sprout again.”

Such a quiet image, and yet so powerful. Life returning where it seemed finished. Hope surviving even after loss.

That single illustration became the heart of this song.

tracks.readme:
_Lamp and Light_

“Your word is a lamp to my foot, and a light for my path.”
I’ve returned to that line many times. Each time, it seems to speak a little differently, yet always with the same quiet clarity.

When I read it, I think first about darkness—not always loud or frightening, but the kind that dulls the edges of things. A darkness where shapes exist without definition, where movement becomes careful and uncertain. In that kind of world, it’s easy to keep moving and still not truly know where you are going.

The image of a lamp feels close and intimate to me. A small circle of light, just enough to see the ground at my feet. Not a grand reveal—just what I need for the next step. In that light, dangers that once felt invisible begin to show themselves. Choices become clearer, not because everything is known, but because enough is known.

Then there is the light—something broader, reaching farther ahead. When I linger on that word, I picture direction rather than safety. Not just avoiding what is near, but seeing where the way is leading. The path begins to take shape. Movement gains purpose. The future, once indistinct, starts to feel real.

Together, those images speak to me of a quiet change:
from stumbling to walking,
from reacting to choosing,
from moving forward blindly to moving forward with intention.

I don’t hear these words as a promise of knowing everything at once, but as an invitation—to walk with just enough light, step by step, toward something clearer, steadier, and filled with hope.

tracks.title: Mercy Shown
tracks.readme:
_Mercy Shown_

This song sits with a familiar story and looks beyond the summary. Jonah is often remembered for running, but his story is really about fear, responsibility, correction, and compassion. He was chosen, overwhelmed, wrong at times — and still heard.

The distance Jonah runs is not measured in miles so much as uncertainty and fear. Between panic and obedience, between judgment and prayer, his story reminds us that even sincere faith can falter, and that faltering does not mean being abandoned.

As I understand it, mercy here is not approval or excuse. It doesn't rush, announce itself, or explain everything. It seems to meet us where we fall, correct us where we wander, and remain when fear makes obedience feel impossible—at least, that's how this story speaks to me.

This song is less about what Jonah did, and more about what God did — and continues to do — for imperfect people trying to obey under the weight of fear.

tracks.title: Ordinary Ways
tracks.readme:
_Ordinary Ways_

I love Peter. In the Gospels, he comes across as so unmistakably real—impetuous, outspoken, imperfect. And yet, we never doubt his love or his faith. He learned, sometimes the easy way, often the hard way. But he learned. And that is what makes him such a powerful example for us.

One moment that captures this so clearly is the account of Jesus washing the apostles’ feet. It reveals the masterful way Jesus taught—often through action.

In this song, I imagine that scene from Peter’s point of view. At first, he resists. Surely this work is beneath Jesus. Then, once corrected, Peter swings in the opposite direction—asking Jesus to wash him completely. In both responses, we see Peter learning in real time.

The lesson I see Peter learning is that greatness is shown through service rather than prominence—though I'm still trying to understand what that really means in practice. And that service, practiced quietly and consistently, speaks more powerfully than the grandest display.

I want to imitate that example—and no doubt fail many times along the way. And that’s why I love Peter. He shows us that you can miss the lesson, stumble forward, and still keep trying until it finally takes root.

tracks.title: Overtone
tracks.readme:
_Overtone_

Psalm 1:2 describes delight in God’s Word as a quiet, continual meditation — reading in an undertone. This song reflects on what that kind of meditation produces. Truth held gently and repeatedly does not remain abstract; it forms roots.

This started from a few lines that were written first, resonated deeply with me and became a foundation in the chorus:


    But Your Word is more than light,
    More than logic polished bright.

    It asks the soul to sing it twice—
    Once in whisper, -- once in life;


The overtone is not performance, but resonance. What is murmured inwardly becomes embodied outwardly. The song is less about proclamation and more about formation — how Scripture, when allowed to settle deeply, reshapes the one who dwells in it.

tracks.name: Valley
tracks.title: In the Valley
tracks.readme:
_In the Valley_
“The Philistines occupied the mountain on one side, and the Israelites occupied the mountain on the other side, with the valley between them.”
— 1 Samuel 17:3

When I read the account of David and Goliath, what caught my attention wasn’t just the giant—it was the valley.

Both armies held the high ground. Neither wanted to step down into that open place of vulnerability. Goliath’s challenge wasn’t only about strength; it was an invitation to leave safety and face fear head-on. No one answered—until David arrived, not as a warrior, but carrying bread.

David had already learned faith in quieter places: alone in the fields, facing danger without an audience. If he felt fear in the valley, it didn’t stop him from entering it. He trusted the God who had walked with him before.

What I had never noticed before was how this moment echoes Psalm 23. Years later, David would write about walking through “the valley of deep shadow” without fear. I can’t help but wonder if this was one of the valleys he had in mind—looking back on his youth and recognizing that Jehovah had been with him in every frightening place, every narrow pass, every moment of weakness.

This song moves between that first valley and later seasons of David’s life—when the battles were no longer public or loud, but internal and lonely. The setting changes, but the truth remains the same: he was never alone in the valley.

Valley is about walking into places of weakness without losing faith—about realizing that long before the stone flew, we were never alone.

tracks.name: Anxious
tracks.title: Stop Being Anxious
tracks.readme:
_Stop Being Anxious_

This was one of the first songs I arranged.

The lyrics aren’t mine. They come directly from scripture, from Jesus’ simple and direct statement: “Stop being anxious.” That sentence matters to me because it doesn’t deny reality. It acknowledges it. It recognizes that anxiety is already present—that the listener is already carrying something heavy.

That has always been true for me.

I overthink. I internalize. Anxiety comes easily, and panic attacks have been part of my life. If that instruction stood alone, I wouldn’t know how to follow it. The ability to live with anxiety—to manage it, to reduce its grip—has come through good doctors, better medication, and the steady encouragement and reminders found in the Bible. Not one thing instead of another. All of it together.

This song centers on one of those reminders: the picture of a bird that doesn’t worry about what it will eat tomorrow. Not because life is easy, but because its care isn’t its own responsibility. And then the quiet, personal reminder that follows—that God cares for us… for me… far more than He does for the birds.

This song isn’t a cure and it isn’t a command shouted from a distance. It’s a gentle interruption—a reminder to pause, breathe, and loosen the grip just a little. Sometimes that’s enough for the moment.

tracks.readme:
_Friends Born for the Storm_

This song grew out of the thought expressed at Proverbs 17:17:
“A true friend shows love at all times, and is a brother who is born for times of distress.”

At first the idea seems simple: when someone we care about faces distress, a real friend rises to the occasion. When the ground gives way and things fall apart, a true friend draws closer rather than pulling away. In that sense, true friends are born for the storm.

But the thought keeps unfolding, to me.

In times of distress we often find that strength comes from more than one place. Alongside loyal friends, we discover the steady support of God himself. Often quietly and without spectacle, he proves to be the most dependable friend of all — the one who does not let us fall when everything else feels uncertain.

And there is another source of strength that many of us recognize. Words we have known for years — passages from the Scriptures — can suddenly take on deeper meaning when life becomes difficult. Like an old friend who understands exactly what to say, those words seem to rise to the occasion just when they are needed most.

This song reflects on those three sources of strength:
friends who stay close, God who holds us steady, and the enduring words that give us courage when the heart is worn.

Together, they remind us that when distress comes, we are not facing the storm alone.

tracks.name: Exquisite
tracks.title: Exquisite Delight
tracks.readme:
_Exquisite Delight_

These verses are dear to many of us. They remind us that we hold onto promises from God about a future that is almost impossible to imagine — and yet we love to try. In thinking about those promises, we begin to realize something wonderful: we don’t have to wait for them to be fulfilled to experience joy. We can find great, even exquisite, delight right now by becoming friends with someone who not only wishes such good things for us, but who is already preparing them.

Before anything else, I should say that this musical setting may not be to everyone’s liking.

While experimenting with different musical styles, I stumbled into this one almost by accident. I’ve always enjoyed the sound of older rock music from the 1960s and 70s — especially the guitar. There’s something about the almost psychedelic tone of a wah pedal and an overdriven tube amplifier, where the sound breaks up in beautifully raw ways. The groove and tone of that era have always brought a smile to my face.

For me, that sense of delight fits these verses.

I also realize that hearing cherished scriptural passages presented in this style may feel unusual — even jarring — to some listeners. That’s understandable. But for me, the joy and groove of this sound capture something of the delight these verses describe. If it causes someone else to smile the way it makes me smile, then the experiment was well worth it.

_He Hears My Voice_

This song was created as a gift for a friend.

My own musical interests tend to lean toward blues, rock, country-rock, and acoustic folk. When I asked her what she enjoyed listening to, she told me—very kindly—that rock was her least favorite. Instead, she shared her love for smoother styles: jazz textures, gentle rhythms, expressive melody, and music that leaves room to breathe. She also shared a verse that’s especially meaningful to her—Psalm 116:1.

So this song was written with her ears and her heart in mind.  The lyrics are straight from scripture.

It was a treat stepping outside my usual habits and shaping something around her taste and the the verse she loves. While it may not be my natural style, that’s part of what made it special. This wasn’t about writing for myself—it was about listening, adapting, and offering something personal in response.
